resources.string: Fortia uses Health Connect for two things:

• Reading the data from your band or watch (for example the Xiaomi Smart Band through Mi Fitness): steps, distance, calories, heart rate, resting heart rate, heart rate variability, sleep, blood oxygen, respiratory rate and workouts. It also reads the weight and body fat recorded by other apps. With the past-data permission it imports up to one year.
• Writing your scale measurements: weight, body fat, bone mass, lean mass, basal metabolic rate and body water. If you delete a measurement in the app, it is also deleted from Health Connect.

Data read from Health Connect is stored only on this phone: it is not uploaded to the optional cloud backup, not used for advertising and not shared with anyone. The app uses it only to show you summaries and charts.
You can revoke any permission at any time in Health Connect; the app stops reading that type of data and deletes its local copy on the next sync.

1. Set the backrest so your knees line up with the pivot point and lower the thigh pad just above your knees.
2. Rest the back of your lower legs on the roller, just above your heels, and hold the handles.
3. Pull your heels down and back under the seat as far as you can.
4. Return slowly until your legs are almost straight.
• Keep the thigh pad snug so your hips don\'t lift.\n• Keep your back against the backrest and control the return; don\'t let the weight snap back.

1. Stand under the shoulder pads with the balls of your feet on the edge of the step, heels hanging off.
2. Straighten your legs, without locking your knees, to lift the weight.
3. Lower your heels slowly as far as is comfortable to stretch your calves.
4. Rise onto your toes as high as you can and hold for a moment at the top.
• Keep your knees straight but not locked: only your ankles move.\n• Pause at the bottom instead of bouncing.

1. Sit with the balls of your feet on the footrest and the knee pad snug on your lower thighs.
2. Lift your heels slightly and release the safety lever.
3. Lower your heels slowly as far as is comfortable.
4. Push up onto your toes as high as you can, pause, and repeat; engage the lever again at the end.
• Only your ankles move; don\'t push with your hands or lean back.\n• Pause at the bottom and at the top instead of bouncing.

1. Sit in the leg press with the balls of your feet on the bottom edge of the platform, heels off.
2. Straighten your legs, without locking your knees, and release the safety handles.
3. Let the platform bring your toes back toward you as far as is comfortable.
4. Push the platform away with your toes as far as you can, pause, and repeat.
• Place your feet firmly so they can\'t slip off the platform.\n• Keep your knees still; only your ankles move.\n• Engage the safety handles before you bend your knees.

1. Stand with the balls of your feet on the edge of the step, bend forward at the hips and set your hips under the pad.
2. Hold the handles with your back flat and your knees almost straight.
3. Lower your heels slowly as far as is comfortable.
4. Rise onto your toes as high as you can and hold for a moment.
• Only your ankles move; keep your hips and knees still.\n• Pause at the bottom instead of bouncing.

1. Sit with your back against the pad and the outside of your knees against the pads, legs together.
2. Hold the handles and keep your back straight.
3. Push your knees out to the sides as far as you can control.
4. Return slowly without letting the plates touch.
• Leaning slightly forward works the glutes more; stay steady either way.\n• Move smoothly; don\'t let the pads snap your legs back together.

1. Set the starting width so you feel a light stretch in your inner thighs, then sit with your back on the pad.
2. Place the inside of your knees against the pads and hold the handles.
3. Squeeze your legs together until the pads meet.
4. Open slowly back to the starting position.
• Choose a starting width that stretches without straining your groin.\n• Keep your back on the pad and avoid jerky movements.

1. Get into position with your chest or forearms on the support and one foot on the footplate.
2. Brace your core and keep your hips square to the machine.
3. Push the footplate back and up by extending your hip until your leg is in line with your body.
4. Squeeze your glute at the top and return slowly; finish your reps, then switch legs.
• Move from the hip, not the lower back: don\'t arch to push higher.\n• Keep your hips level; don\'t twist to the side.

1. Sit with your upper back against the pad and fasten the belt or pad across your hips.
2. Place your feet flat, hip-width apart, so your shins are vertical at the top.
3. Drive through your heels to lift your hips until your knees, hips and shoulders are in line.
4. Squeeze your glutes at the top, then lower under control.
• Keep your chin tucked and ribs down; don\'t arch your lower back at the top.\n• If you feel it mostly in your hamstrings, bring your feet a little closer.

1. Sit with your feet on the footrest and the pad on your upper back; fasten the belt if there is one.
2. Cross your arms on your chest or hold the handles.
3. Push back against the pad by extending your back until your torso is upright or slightly reclined.
4. Return slowly to the start.
• Move smoothly and stop at a slight lean back; don\'t force the extension.\n• Use a moderate weight: this is a control exercise, not a max lift.

1. Lie face down on the pad with your hips at its edge and your legs hanging down.
2. Hook your ankles under the roller (or strap) and hold the handles.
3. Squeeze your glutes to swing your legs up until they're in line with your body.
4. Lower them slowly under control.
• Lift with your glutes and keep the swing controlled; don\'t kick.\n• Stop at body level: going higher only loads your lower back.

1. Set the seat so the handles are at chest height and hook your feet under the rollers if there are any.
2. Hold the handles and sit with your back against the pad.
3. Crunch forward by curling your ribs toward your hips as you breathe out.
4. Return slowly until your abs are stretched, without letting the weight rest.
• Curl your spine; don\'t just pull with your arms or bend at the hips.\n• Keep the movement slow and controlled.

1. Set the starting angle to one side and sit with your knees or legs against the pads, depending on the model.
2. Place your chest or arms against the pads, hold the handles and keep your back straight.
3. Turn your torso in a controlled arc from your waist, using your obliques, not your arms.
4. Return slowly; finish your reps, then set the machine to the other side.
• Turn from your waist and keep the movement slow; don\'t swing.\n• Use a light weight and a range you can control.

1. Set the seat so your upper arms rest flat on the pad and your elbows line up with the pivot point.
2. Grip the handles with your palms facing up.
3. Curl the handles toward your shoulders, squeezing your biceps.
4. Lower slowly until your arms are almost straight.
• Keep your elbows on the pad and don\'t rise off the seat to help.\n• Control the lowering; don\'t let the weight drop.

1. Set the seat so your upper arms rest on the pad and your elbows line up with the pivot point.
2. Grip the handles with your elbows bent.
3. Straighten your arms by pushing the handles until your elbows are fully extended.
4. Return slowly to the start.
• Keep your elbows fixed on the pad; only your forearms move.\n• Don\'t lean forward to push the weight.

1. Set the seat so that, with your elbows bent, the handles are at about lower-chest height.
2. Sit with your back against the pad, fasten the thigh pad if there is one, and grip the handles.
3. Push the handles down until your arms are straight, keeping your elbows close to your body.
4. Return slowly until your elbows are bent about 90 degrees.
• Keep your shoulders down and back; don\'t let them roll forward.\n• Sitting upright works the triceps more; leaning forward shifts work to the chest.

1. Select the counterweight: the more weight, the more help you get.
2. Kneel or stand on the platform and grip the top handles wider than your shoulders, palms facing away.
3. Pull yourself up until your chin is above the handles, driving your elbows down toward your sides.
4. Lower slowly until your arms are straight.

• Aim to reduce the counterweight over time: less assistance means more strength.\n• Start each rep from straight arms with your shoulders down, not shrugged.\n• Step down carefully: hold the handles until both feet are on the steps.

1. Select the counterweight: the more weight, the more help you get.
2. Kneel or stand on the platform and grip the handles shoulder-width apart, palms facing you.
3. Pull yourself up until your chin is above your hands, keeping your elbows in front of you.
4. Lower slowly until your arms are straight.

• Aim to reduce the counterweight over time: less assistance means more strength.\n• Don\'t swing or kick; keep your body still and your core tight.\n• Step down carefully: hold the handles until both feet are on the steps.

1. Select the counterweight: the more weight, the more help you get.
2. Grip the dip handles, then kneel or stand on the platform with your arms straight.
3. Lower yourself by bending your elbows until your upper arms are about parallel to the floor.
4. Push back up until your arms are straight.

• Aim to reduce the counterweight over time: less assistance means more strength.\n• Keep your shoulders down and don\'t go deeper than is comfortable for them.\n• Lean slightly forward for more chest; stay upright for more triceps.

1. Set the seat so the pad rests on your forehead or the back of your head, depending on the direction you train.
2. Sit with your back straight, hold the handles and keep your shoulders still.
3. Move your head slowly against the pad through a small, comfortable range.
4. Return slowly to the neutral position.
• Use a light weight and slow, smooth reps; never jerk your neck.\n• Keep the range small and free of discomfort.

1. Set the thigh pad so your legs fit snugly under it.
2. Grip the bar a little wider than your shoulders, palms facing away, and sit down.
3. Pull the bar down to your upper chest, driving your elbows down and back.
4. Let the bar rise slowly until your arms are straight.
• Lean back only slightly and keep your chest up; don\'t swing your body.\n• Don\'t pull the bar behind your neck.

1. Attach a close-grip (V) handle and set the thigh pad so your legs fit snugly under it.
2. Grip the handle with your palms facing each other and sit down with your arms straight.
3. Pull the handle to your upper chest, keeping your elbows close to your body.
4. Let it rise slowly until your arms are straight and your lats stretch.
• Keep your chest up and lean back only slightly.\n• Pull with your elbows; don\'t yank with your arms or swing.

1. Attach a V-handle (or a bar), sit down and place your feet on the footrests, knees slightly bent.
2. Grip the handle and sit tall with your arms straight and your back neutral.
3. Pull the handle to your stomach, driving your elbows back and squeezing your shoulder blades.
4. Return slowly until your arms are straight, letting your shoulders reach forward slightly.
• Keep your torso still; don\'t rock back and forth to move the weight.\n• Keep your chest up and your shoulders down.

1. Attach a single handle at about waist or chest height and grip it with one hand.
2. Face the pulley in a staggered stance (or sit down), with your arm straight and your core braced.
3. Pull the handle to your side, driving your elbow back close to your body.
4. Return slowly, letting your shoulder reach forward; finish your reps and switch arms.
• Keep your hips and shoulders square; don\'t twist your torso to pull.\n• Pull with your elbow and keep your shoulder down.

1. Attach a straight bar or rope to the high pulley and stand facing it, a step back, feet hip-width apart.
2. Grip the bar shoulder-width apart, hinge slightly at the hips and keep your arms straight.
3. Sweep the bar down in an arc to your thighs, using your lats.
4. Let it rise slowly back to about head height.
• Keep your elbows fixed in a slight bend; don\'t turn it into a triceps pushdown.\n• Keep your torso still; don\'t bob up and down.

1. Set both pulleys high, take a handle in each hand and step forward between them in a staggered stance.
2. Lean slightly forward with your arms open and a slight bend in your elbows.
3. Bring the handles down and together in front of your lower chest in a wide arc.
4. Squeeze, then let your arms open slowly until you feel a stretch across your chest.
• Keep the same elbow bend throughout; the movement happens at the shoulders.\n• Don\'t let the cables pull your arms too far back.

1. Set both pulleys at the lowest position, take a handle in each hand and step forward between them.
2. Stand tall with your arms down and slightly out to the sides, palms forward, elbows slightly bent.
3. Bring the handles up and together in front of your upper chest in a wide arc.
4. Lower them slowly back out to your sides.
• Keep the slight elbow bend fixed; don\'t curl the handles up.\n• Keep your shoulders down and your chest up.

1. Set both pulleys at about chest height, take a handle in each hand and step forward in a staggered stance.
2. Open your arms out to the sides at chest level, elbows slightly bent.
3. Bring the handles together in front of your chest in a wide hugging arc.
4. Open slowly until you feel a stretch in your chest, keeping tension on the cables.
• Keep your elbows slightly bent and fixed: it\'s a fly, not a press.\n• Brace your core so your body doesn\'t sway with the cables.

1. Attach a rope to a pulley at about face height or slightly above.
2. Grip each end of the rope, thumbs toward you, and step back until your arms are straight.
3. Pull the rope toward your face, splitting the ends apart and driving your elbows out and high.
4. Finish with your hands beside your ears, then return slowly.
• Keep your elbows at or above shoulder height and squeeze your upper back.\n• Use a light weight; don\'t lean back to pull.

1. Set a pulley at the lowest position with a single handle and stand side-on to it.
2. Grip the handle with the hand farther from the machine, the cable crossing in front of your body.
3. Raise your arm out to the side until your elbow reaches shoulder height, elbow slightly bent.
4. Lower slowly; finish your reps and switch sides.
• Lead with your elbow and keep your shoulder down, away from your ear.\n• Don\'t lean or swing to lift the weight.

1. Attach a straight or angled bar to the high pulley and stand facing it, feet hip-width apart.
2. Grip the bar palms down and bring your elbows to your sides, forearms about parallel to the floor.
3. Push the bar down until your arms are fully straight.
4. Let it rise slowly until your forearms are just above parallel.
• Keep your elbows pinned to your sides; only your forearms move.\n• Don\'t lean over the bar or use your body weight to push.

1. Attach a rope to the high pulley and stand facing it, feet hip-width apart.
2. Grip the rope ends with your palms facing each other and bring your elbows to your sides.
3. Push the rope down, spreading the ends apart at the bottom, until your arms are straight.
4. Let the rope rise slowly until your forearms are just above parallel.
• Keep your elbows still at your sides throughout.\n• Spread the rope at the bottom to finish each rep; don\'t lean forward.

1. Attach a rope to a low or middle pulley, grip it and turn your back to the machine.
2. Step forward into a staggered stance, hands behind your head and elbows pointing up.
3. Straighten your arms overhead until your elbows are fully extended.
4. Bend your elbows slowly to bring the rope back behind your head.
• Keep your elbows close to your head and still; only your forearms move.\n• Brace your core so your lower back doesn\'t arch.

1. Attach a straight or EZ bar to the low pulley and stand facing it, feet hip-width apart.
2. Grip the bar palms up, shoulder-width apart, with your arms straight and elbows at your sides.
3. Curl the bar toward your shoulders, squeezing your biceps.
4. Lower slowly until your arms are straight.
• Keep your elbows at your sides; don\'t let them drift forward.\n• Don\'t lean back or swing to lift the weight.

1. Attach a rope to a low pulley and hold one end in each hand, palms facing each other.
2. Stand tall facing the machine with your elbows by your sides.
3. Curl the rope up toward your shoulders, palms still facing in.
4. Lower slowly until your arms are straight.
• Keep your elbows pinned to your sides; don\'t swing your body.\n• The neutral grip works the forearms and the brachialis more than a regular curl.

1. Attach a rope to the high pulley and kneel facing the machine, about an arm's length away.
2. Hold the rope ends beside your head and hinge forward slightly at the hips.
3. Crunch down by curling your ribs toward your hips until your elbows approach your thighs.
4. Return slowly until your abs are stretched, keeping your hips still.
• Curl your spine; don\'t sit back on your heels or pull with your arms.\n• Keep your hips high and in the same place throughout.

1. Set a pulley at the highest position with a handle and stand side-on to it, feet wider than your shoulders.
2. Grip the handle with both hands, arms almost straight, above the shoulder nearest the machine.
3. Pull it diagonally down and across your body to outside your opposite knee, rotating your torso.
4. Return slowly along the same path; finish your reps and switch sides.
• Pivot on your back foot and turn from your torso and hips, keeping your arms long.\n• Control the return; don\'t let the cable pull you back.

1. Set a handle on a low pulley and stand side-on to it, feet wider than your shoulders.
2. Bend your knees a little and hold the handle with both hands beside the knee nearest the machine.
3. Pull it up diagonally across your body to above the opposite shoulder, turning your trunk and pivoting your back foot.
4. Return slowly along the same line; switch sides after the set.
• Keep your arms long and move with your trunk and hips, not just your arms.\n• Brace your abs so the turn stays controlled.

1. Set a handle at chest height and stand side-on to the machine, a step away so the cable is tight.
2. Hold the handle with both hands at your chest, feet hip-width apart, knees soft.
3. Press it straight out in front of you and hold for a moment without letting your body turn.
4. Bring it back to your chest under control; switch sides after the set.
• Your trunk resists the pull: hips and shoulders stay square to the front.\n• Brace your abs and breathe out as you press.

1. Attach a rope to the low pulley, face away from the machine and grip the rope between your legs.
2. Walk forward a couple of steps and stand with your feet a little wider than hip-width.
3. Hinge at the hips, pushing them back with a flat back, until you feel a stretch in your hamstrings.
4. Drive your hips forward to stand up tall, squeezing your glutes at the top.
• It\'s a hip hinge, not a squat: keep your knees soft and push your hips back.\n• Don\'t lean back at the top; just stand tall.

1. Attach an ankle strap to the low pulley and fasten it around one ankle.
2. Face the machine, hold the frame for support and hinge slightly forward.
3. Kick the strapped leg back by extending your hip, knee slightly bent.
4. Squeeze your glute, return slowly, and switch legs after your reps.
• Don\'t arch your lower back to lift the leg higher.\n• Keep your hips square; don\'t rotate your leg outward.

1. Fasten an ankle strap to a low pulley and to the ankle nearest the machine, and stand side-on to it.
2. Hold the machine for balance and let the cable draw your working leg out to the side.
3. Bring the leg in across the front of your standing leg, keeping it straight.
4. Return slowly out to the side; switch legs after the set.
• Stand tall and keep your hips level; only the leg moves.\n• Use a light weight and a slow, controlled pace.

1. Fasten an ankle strap to a low pulley and to the ankle farthest from the machine, and stand side-on to it.
2. Hold the machine for balance; the cable crosses in front of your standing leg.
3. Lift the working leg out to the side, straight, with your toes pointing forward.
4. Lower it slowly back; switch legs after the set.
• Don\'t lean away from the machine to lift higher: keep your trunk upright.\n• Lead with the heel, not the toes, to keep the work in your glutes.

1. Set the bar at about shoulder height and the safety stops just below your lowest squat depth.
2. Step under the bar, rest it on your upper back and place your feet slightly forward, shoulder-width apart.
3. Rotate the bar to unhook it, then squat down until your thighs are about parallel to the floor.
4. Drive up through your whole foot to standing; rotate the bar to hook it back on at the end.
• The bar moves on a fixed path: find a foot position that feels comfortable for your knees and back.\n• Keep your chest up and your knees in line with your toes.

1. Place a flat bench under the bar so it lines up with your mid-chest, and set the safety stops at chest level.
2. Lie down, feet flat, shoulder blades back and down, and grip the bar slightly wider than your shoulders.
3. Rotate the bar to unhook it and lower it under control to your mid-chest.
4. Press it back up until your arms are almost straight; rotate it to hook it back on at the end.
• Check the bench position before loading: the fixed path should land on your mid-chest.\n• Keep your elbows at about 45 degrees from your body, not flared out.

1. Set an incline bench at 30–45 degrees under the bar so it lines up with your upper chest; set the safety stops.
2. Lie back, feet flat, shoulder blades back and down, and grip the bar slightly wider than your shoulders.
3. Rotate the bar to unhook it and lower it under control to your upper chest.
4. Press back up until your arms are almost straight; hook the bar back on at the end.
• A lower incline keeps more of the work on the chest; a steep one shifts it to the shoulders.\n• Don\'t bounce the bar off your chest.

1. Place a bench with an upright back under the bar so the bar comes down just in front of your face.
2. Sit with your back against the pad and grip the bar slightly wider than your shoulders.
3. Rotate the bar to unhook it and lower it to about chin height.
4. Press it up until your arms are almost straight; hook the bar back on at the end.
• Keep your lower back against the pad; don\'t arch to push.\n• Set the safety stops so the bar can\'t come down onto your head.

1. Set the bar at about shoulder height, step under it and rest it on your upper back.
2. Unhook the bar and take a long stance: one foot forward, the other back on its toes.
3. Lower your back knee toward the floor until your front thigh is about parallel to it.
4. Push through your front foot to rise; finish your reps, then switch legs.
• Keep your torso upright and your front knee in line with your toes.\n• Keep your feet in place for the whole set; the bar\'s fixed path keeps you balanced.

1. Set a bench behind the Smith machine and the bar at shoulder height; get under it with the bar on your upper back.
2. Step one foot forward and rest the top of the other foot on the bench behind you.
3. Unrack the bar and lower straight down until your front thigh is about parallel.
4. Push up through your front foot; finish the set and switch legs.
• Place your front foot far enough forward that your knee stays over your foot.\n• Keep your trunk upright and most of your weight on the front leg.

1. Set the bar low, sit on the floor with your upper back against a bench and the padded bar over your hips.
2. Place your feet flat, hip-width apart, and rotate the bar to unhook it.
3. Drive through your heels to raise your hips until your knees, hips and shoulders are in line.
4. Squeeze your glutes at the top, lower under control and hook the bar back on at the end.
• Use a pad on the bar and keep your chin tucked.\n• Don\'t arch your lower back at the top; finish the movement with your glutes.

1. Set the bar at mid-thigh height and grip it just outside your thighs, feet hip-width apart.
2. Unrack it and stand tall with your knees soft.
3. Push your hips back and slide the bar down your thighs until you feel a stretch in your hamstrings, back flat.
4. Drive your hips forward to stand back up.
• The bar runs straight down the rails: stand so it stays close to your legs.\n• Stop when your back would start to round, usually around mid-shin.

1. Set the bar low on the rails and grip it a little wider than your shoulders.
2. Unrack it and hinge forward at the hips with your back flat and your knees soft.
3. Pull the bar straight up to your lower ribs, squeezing your shoulder blades together.
4. Lower it slowly until your arms are straight.
• Keep your torso still: the bar moves, not your back.\n• Lead with your elbows and don\'t shrug.

1. Set the bar at mid-thigh height and grip it shoulder-width apart.
2. Unrack it and stand tall with your arms straight.
3. Lift your shoulders straight up toward your ears and squeeze for a moment.
4. Lower them slowly all the way down.
• Move straight up and down; don\'t roll your shoulders.\n• Keep your arms straight: the elbows don\'t bend.

1. Place a step or plate under the bar, set the bar at shoulder height and rest it on your upper back.
2. Stand with the balls of your feet on the edge of the step, heels hanging off, and unhook the bar.
3. Lower your heels slowly as far as is comfortable.
4. Rise onto your toes as high as you can, pause, and repeat; hook the bar back on at the end.
• Keep your knees straight but not locked; only your ankles move.\n• Pause at the bottom instead of bouncing.

1. Lie on a flat bench with your eyes under the bar and your feet flat on the floor.
2. Grip the bar slightly wider than your shoulders and pull your shoulder blades back and down.
3. Unrack the bar and lower it under control to your mid-chest.
4. Press it back up over your shoulders until your arms are straight, then rack it.
• Keep your shoulder blades back and down and your feet planted.\n• Don\'t bounce the bar off your chest; keep your elbows at about 45 degrees.\n• Use a spotter or safety arms for heavy sets.

1. Set the bench at 30–45 degrees and lie back with your eyes under the bar, feet flat.
2. Grip the bar slightly wider than your shoulders and set your shoulder blades back and down.
3. Unrack the bar and lower it under control to your upper chest, just below the collarbones.
4. Press it back up until your arms are straight, then rack it.
• Keep your hips on the bench and your shoulder blades pinned.\n• Don\'t flare your elbows straight out to the sides; use a spotter for heavy sets.

1. Hook your legs under the pads of a decline bench and lie back with your eyes under the bar.
2. Grip the bar slightly wider than your shoulders, shoulder blades back and down.
3. Unrack the bar (ideally with a spotter) and lower it under control to your lower chest.
4. Press it back up until your arms are straight, then rack it.
• Have a spotter hand you the bar and help you rack it: the decline makes this awkward.\n• Lower slowly; don\'t bounce the bar off your chest.

1. Lie on a flat bench with your eyes under the bar and your feet flat.
2. Grip the bar about shoulder-width apart (no narrower) and set your shoulder blades.
3. Unrack the bar and lower it to your lower chest, keeping your elbows close to your body.
4. Press it back up until your arms are straight, then rack it.
• A shoulder-width grip is enough; a very narrow grip strains the wrists.\n• Keep your elbows tucked and your wrists straight above your elbows.

1. Lie on a flat bench and grip the bar about shoulder-width apart, arms straight over your shoulders.
2. Lower the bar toward your chin by bending your elbows, letting them point toward your feet.
3. Stop a few centimetres above your chin or upper chest.
4. Press back up to straight arms.
• It\'s a cross between a close-grip press and a skull crusher: keep the elbows in, not flared.\n• Use less weight than for a bench press, and a spotter or safety pins.

1. Set the bar in a rack at upper-chest height and grip it just outside your shoulders.
2. Unrack it onto the front of your shoulders, step back and brace your glutes and core.
3. Press the bar straight up, moving your head back slightly to let it pass, until your arms are straight.
4. Lower it under control to the front of your shoulders.
• Squeeze your glutes and abs so your lower back doesn\'t arch.\n• Finish with the bar over your mid-foot and your head between your arms.

1. Wedge one end of a bar in a landmine (or a corner) and load the other end.
2. Stand facing it in a split stance, holding the loaded end at your shoulder with one hand.
3. Press the bar up and forward until your arm is straight.
4. Lower it back to your shoulder under control; switch sides after the set.
• Brace your abs and don\'t lean back; the bar\'s arc does the work.\n• Easy on the shoulders: a good option if overhead presses bother you.

1. Set the bar in a rack at about armpit height and the safety arms just below your lowest squat depth.
2. Step under the bar, rest it on your upper back (not your neck), grip it firmly and stand up to unrack it.
3. Step back, feet shoulder-width apart and toes slightly out, and squat down to parallel or below.
4. Drive up through your whole foot to standing, then walk the bar back into the rack.
• Brace your core before each rep and keep your chest up.\n• Keep your knees in line with your toes and your heels on the floor.\n• Use safety arms or a spotter when you go heavy.

1. Set the bar in a rack at shoulder height and step under it so it rests on the front of your shoulders.
2. Hold it with your fingertips under the bar (or arms crossed), elbows high, and stand up to unrack it.
3. Step back, feet shoulder-width apart, and squat down keeping your torso upright and elbows up.
4. Drive up through your whole foot to standing, then rack the bar.
• Keep your elbows high so the bar doesn\'t roll forward.\n• Stay upright and let your knees travel forward over your toes.

1. Set the bar in a rack at about waist height.
2. Hold it in the crook of your elbows, hands clasped in front of your chest, and step back.
3. Squat down with your chest up until your thighs are at least parallel.
4. Drive back up, keeping your elbows high.
• A pad or towel round the bar makes it easier on your arms.\n• The bar in front keeps you upright: brace your abs and upper back.

1. Stand with your mid-foot under the bar, feet hip-width apart.
2. Hinge down and grip the bar just outside your legs; bend your knees until your shins touch the bar.
3. Flatten your back, lift your chest and pull the slack out of the bar.
4. Push the floor away and stand up with the bar close to your legs, hips and shoulders rising together.
5. Lower the bar to the floor by pushing your hips back, bending your knees once it passes them.
• Keep your back neutral; never round it to reach the bar.\n• Keep the bar in contact with your legs the whole way.\n• Finish standing tall; don\'t lean back at the top.

1. Take a wide stance, toes pointed out, with the bar over your mid-foot and close to your shins.
2. Squat down with a straight back and grip the bar shoulder-width apart, arms inside your knees.
3. Push your knees out over your toes, lift your chest and pull the slack out of the bar.
4. Push the floor apart and stand up with the bar close, bringing your hips forward to finish.
5. Lower the bar to the floor under control along the same path.
• Keep your knees tracking over your toes; don\'t let them collapse inward.\n• Your torso stays more upright than in a conventional deadlift; keep your back neutral.

1. Set the safety pins in a rack so the bar rests just above or below your knees.
2. Stand close with your feet hip-width apart and grip the bar just outside your legs.
3. With your back flat and chest up, drive your hips forward and stand tall with the bar.
4. Lower it back to the pins under control.
• Pull your shoulders back at the top without leaning back.\n• You can lift more than in a deadlift: build up the weight gradually.

1. Start standing with the bar at your hips, hands shoulder-width apart and feet hip-width apart.
2. With your knees slightly bent and fixed, push your hips back and lower the bar along your thighs.
3. Go down until you feel a strong stretch in your hamstrings, usually just below the knees, back flat.
4. Drive your hips forward to stand back up, squeezing your glutes.
• Unlike a deadlift, the bar doesn\'t touch the floor between reps and your knees barely bend.\n• Keep the bar close to your legs and your back neutral; stop when your hips can\'t go further back.

1. Rest the bar on your upper back as for a back squat, unrack it and step back, feet hip-width apart.
2. Unlock your knees slightly and brace your core.
3. Push your hips back and lower your torso with a flat back until you feel a strong stretch in your hamstrings.
4. Drive your hips forward to return to standing.
• Start light: the load sits far from your hips, so it feels heavier than it looks.\n• Keep your back neutral; stop before it starts to round.

1. Sit on the end of a bench with the bar on your upper back and your feet wide and flat.
2. Brace your abs and keep your back flat.
3. Hinge forward from the hips as far as you can without rounding your back.
4. Come back up to sitting tall.
• Start light: your lower back does most of the work.\n• Move only at the hips, with your head in line with your spine.

1. Rest the bar on your upper back, unrack it and step back to a spot with room to step forward.
2. Stand tall with your feet hip-width apart and brace your core.
3. Step forward with one leg and lower your back knee toward the floor until both knees are bent about 90 degrees.
4. Push through your front foot to return to the start, then alternate legs.
• Keep your torso upright and your front knee in line with your toes.\n• Take a long enough step that your front heel stays down; find your balance before each step.

1. Sit on the floor with your upper back against a bench and roll a padded barbell over your hips.
2. Place your feet flat, hip-width apart, so your shins are vertical at the top.
3. Drive through your heels to lift your hips until your knees, hips and shoulders are in line.
4. Squeeze your glutes at the top, then lower under control.
• Keep your chin tucked and ribs down; don\'t arch your lower back to get higher.\n• Use a bar pad and hold the bar so it doesn\'t roll.

1. Lie on your back on the floor, knees bent and feet flat, hip-width apart.
2. Roll a padded barbell over your hips and hold it in place with both hands.
3. Drive through your heels to lift your hips until your knees, hips and shoulders are in line.
4. Squeeze your glutes at the top, then lower until your glutes lightly touch the floor.
• The range is shorter than in a hip thrust: focus on a strong squeeze at the top.\n• Don\'t arch your lower back; keep your ribs down.

1. Hold the bar with an overhand grip slightly wider than your shoulders, feet hip-width apart.
2. Hinge at the hips, knees slightly bent, until your torso is at about 45 degrees or lower, back flat.
3. Pull the bar to your lower chest or upper stomach, driving your elbows back.
4. Lower it under control until your arms are straight, keeping your torso still.
• Keep your back flat and your torso angle fixed; don\'t stand up to move the weight.\n• Squeeze your shoulder blades at the top and don\'t jerk the bar.

1. Stand with the bar over your mid-foot and grip it overhand, slightly wider than your shoulders.
2. Hinge until your torso is roughly parallel to the floor, back flat and knees slightly bent.
3. Pull the bar explosively from the floor to your lower chest or upper stomach.
4. Lower it back to the floor and let it settle completely before the next rep.
• Every rep starts from a dead stop on the floor; don\'t bounce it.\n• Keep your torso parallel and still; only your arms and shoulder blades move.

1. Load the T-bar (or a barbell in a landmine) and straddle it, feet shoulder-width apart.
2. Grip the handle with both hands and hinge at the hips until your torso is at about 45 degrees, back flat.
3. Pull the handle toward your chest, driving your elbows back and squeezing your shoulder blades.
4. Lower it under control until your arms are straight.
• Keep your chest up and your back flat; don\'t round at the bottom.\n• Don\'t use your legs and hips to heave the weight up.

1. Stand tall holding the bar in front of your thighs with an overhand grip about shoulder-width apart.
2. Pull the bar up close to your body, leading with your elbows.
3. Stop when your elbows reach about shoulder height, with the bar around chest level.
4. Lower it slowly to the start.
• A shoulder-width (not narrow) grip and stopping at shoulder height are easier on your shoulders.\n• Keep the bar close to your body and don\'t swing.

1. Stand tall holding the bar in front of your thighs, hands just outside your hips.
2. Shrug your shoulders straight up toward your ears as high as you can.
3. Hold for a moment at the top.
4. Lower your shoulders slowly to the start.
• Move straight up and down; don\'t roll your shoulders.\n• Keep your arms straight; don\'t bend your elbows to lift.

1. Stand tall holding the bar with an underhand grip, hands shoulder-width apart, arms straight.
2. Keep your elbows at your sides and curl the bar toward your shoulders.
3. Squeeze your biceps at the top.
4. Lower slowly until your arms are straight.
• Don\'t swing your body or lean back to lift the bar.\n• Keep your elbows still; don\'t let them drift forward.

1. Stand tall holding the EZ bar on its angled grips, palms up, arms straight.
2. Keep your elbows at your sides and curl the bar toward your shoulders.
3. Squeeze your biceps at the top.
4. Lower slowly until your arms are straight.
• The angled grip is easier on the wrists than a straight bar.\n• Don\'t swing or lean back; keep your elbows still.

1. Set the preacher bench seat so your armpits rest snugly over the top of the pad.
2. Rest the back of your upper arms on the pad and hold the EZ bar on its angled grips, palms up.
3. Curl the bar up until your forearms are about vertical.
4. Lower slowly until your arms are almost straight.
• Control the bottom: don\'t let the weight drop into a locked elbow.\n• Keep your upper arms on the pad; don\'t lift your shoulders to help.

1. Hold a barbell or EZ bar with an overhand grip (palms down), hands shoulder-width apart.
2. Stand tall with your elbows by your sides.
3. Curl the bar up toward your shoulders, keeping your wrists straight.
4. Lower slowly until your arms are straight.
• Use less weight than for a normal curl.\n• Keep your elbows still and don\'t swing your body.

1. Lie on a flat bench holding an EZ bar or barbell above your chest, arms straight, hands about shoulder-width.
2. Tilt your arms slightly back toward your head and keep your upper arms still.
3. Bend your elbows to lower the bar toward your forehead or just behind your head.
4. Straighten your arms to press it back up.
• Keep your elbows pointing up, not flaring out.\n• Lower slowly and with control: the bar travels toward your head.

1. Sit on a bench holding a barbell palms up, forearms on your thighs and wrists just past your knees.
2. Let the bar roll down toward your fingertips as you lower your wrists.
3. Curl your wrists up as far as you can, squeezing your forearms.
4. Lower slowly and repeat.
• Only your wrists move; keep your forearms flat on your thighs.\n• Use a light weight and a full, controlled range.

1. Sit on a bench holding a barbell palms down, forearms on your thighs and wrists just past your knees.
2. Lower the back of your hands slowly toward the floor.
3. Raise your knuckles as far as you can by extending your wrists.
4. Lower slowly and repeat.
• Use less weight than for wrist curls: these muscles are weaker.\n• Keep your forearms still on your thighs.

1. Wedge one end of a bar in a landmine and hold the other end with both hands at chest height, arms long.
2. Stand facing it with your feet wider than your shoulders.
3. Turn your trunk to bring the bar down to one hip in an arc, pivoting on your back foot.
4. Bring it back up through the middle and down to the other hip.
• Keep your arms nearly straight and turn from your trunk and hips.\n• Control the bar all the way; don\'t let it pull you.

1. Sit on the end of a flat bench with the dumbbells on your thighs, then lie back bringing them to your chest.
2. Plant your feet, set your shoulder blades back and down, and hold the dumbbells beside your chest.
3. Press them up until your arms are straight over your chest.
4. Lower them slowly until your elbows are slightly below the bench or you feel a good stretch.
• Keep your elbows at about 45 degrees from your body.\n• To finish, bring the dumbbells to your chest and sit up with them on your thighs instead of dropping them.

1. Set the bench at 30–45 degrees, sit with the dumbbells on your thighs and lie back bringing them to your chest.
2. Plant your feet and set your shoulder blades back and down.
3. Press the dumbbells up over your upper chest until your arms are straight.
4. Lower them slowly to the sides of your upper chest.
• Keep your elbows slightly tucked, not straight out to the sides.\n• Bring the dumbbells to your thighs as you sit up at the end; don\'t drop them.

1. Lie on a flat bench with a dumbbell in each hand, arms straight above your chest, palms facing each other.
2. Bend your elbows slightly and keep that angle.
3. Open your arms out to the sides in a wide arc until you feel a stretch in your chest.
4. Bring the dumbbells back together above your chest along the same arc.
• Don\'t lower the weights below the bench; stop at a comfortable stretch.\n• Keep the elbow bend fixed: bending more turns it into a press.

1. Lie on a flat bench (along or across it) and hold one dumbbell with both hands above your chest.
2. Keep a slight bend in your elbows and brace your core.
3. Lower the dumbbell in an arc behind your head until you feel a stretch in your chest and lats.
4. Pull it back over your chest along the same arc.
• Only go as far back as is comfortable for your shoulders.\n• Keep your hips down and avoid arching your lower back.

1. Sit on a bench with an upright back and hold the dumbbells at shoulder height, palms forward.
2. Plant your feet and keep your back against the pad.
3. Press the dumbbells up until your arms are straight overhead.
4. Lower them slowly back to shoulder height.
• Don\'t arch your lower back; keep your core tight.\n• Keep your forearms vertical under the dumbbells.

1. Sit on a bench with an upright back, holding the dumbbells in front of your shoulders, palms facing you.
2. Press up while rotating your palms to face forward.
3. Finish with your arms straight overhead.
4. Lower slowly while rotating back to the start, palms facing you.
• Make the rotation smooth and continuous through the whole press.\n• Keep your back against the pad and use less weight than for a regular press.

1. Stand tall with a dumbbell in each hand at your sides, palms facing in, elbows slightly bent.
2. Raise your arms out to the sides until they reach shoulder height.
3. Pause briefly at the top.
4. Lower slowly to your sides.
• Lead with your elbows and keep your shoulders away from your ears.\n• Use a weight you can lift without swinging or leaning back.

1. Stand tall with the dumbbells in front of your thighs, palms facing your body or each other.
2. Raise one or both arms straight in front of you, elbows slightly bent.
3. Stop when your arms reach shoulder height.
4. Lower slowly to the start.
• Don\'t swing or lean back to lift the weights.\n• Going above shoulder height adds little; keep the movement controlled.

1. Hinge forward until your torso is nearly parallel to the floor (or lie chest-down on an incline bench).
2. Let the dumbbells hang below your shoulders, palms facing each other, elbows slightly bent.
3. Raise your arms out to the sides until they're in line with your body.
4. Lower slowly to the start.
• Lead with your elbows and keep your shoulders down; don\'t squeeze your shoulder blades hard.\n• Use a light weight and keep your back flat; don\'t swing.

1. Place one knee and the same-side hand on a flat bench, back flat and roughly parallel to the floor.
2. Hold a dumbbell in the other hand, arm straight below your shoulder.
3. Pull the dumbbell toward your hip, driving your elbow back close to your body.
4. Lower it slowly until your arm is straight; finish your reps and switch sides.
• Keep your back flat and your shoulders level; don\'t twist to lift the weight.\n• Pull toward your hip rather than straight up to your chest.

1. Set a bench to a low incline and lie face down on it with your chest on the pad, feet on the floor.
2. Let the dumbbells hang straight down, palms facing each other.
3. Row them up beside your ribs, squeezing your shoulder blades together.
4. Lower slowly until your arms are straight.
• The bench supports your back, so you can focus on the pull.\n• Keep your chest on the pad; don\'t lift off to swing the weight.

1. Stand tall with a dumbbell in each hand at your sides, palms facing in.
2. Shrug your shoulders straight up toward your ears as high as you can.
3. Hold for a moment at the top.
4. Lower your shoulders slowly to the start.
• Move straight up and down; don\'t roll your shoulders.\n• Keep your arms straight and your head neutral.

1. Stand tall with a dumbbell in each hand, arms straight at your sides, palms facing forward.
2. Keep your elbows at your sides and curl the dumbbells toward your shoulders, together or alternating.
3. Squeeze your biceps at the top.
4. Lower slowly until your arms are straight.
• Don\'t swing your body or let your elbows drift forward.\n• Lower under control; the way down counts too.

1. Stand tall with a dumbbell in each hand at your sides, palms facing your body.
2. Keep your palms facing in and curl the dumbbells toward your shoulders.
3. Squeeze at the top with your thumbs pointing up.
4. Lower slowly until your arms are straight.
• Keep the neutral grip (palms facing each other) the whole way.\n• Keep your elbows at your sides and don\'t swing.

1. Set a bench at 45–60 degrees and lie back with a dumbbell in each hand, arms hanging straight down.
2. Turn your palms forward and keep your upper arms vertical.
3. Curl the dumbbells toward your shoulders without moving your elbows forward.
4. Lower slowly until your arms are fully straight.
• Keep your head and back against the bench.\n• The stretched start is the point of this curl: use less weight than standing.

1. Sit on a bench with your feet wide apart and a dumbbell in one hand.
2. Rest the back of that upper arm against your inner thigh, arm straight, palm up.
3. Curl the dumbbell toward your shoulder, keeping your upper arm still.
4. Lower slowly until your arm is straight; finish your reps and switch arms.
• Don\'t lean back or use your thigh to push your arm up.\n• Squeeze your biceps for a moment at the top.

1. Stand with a dumbbell in each hand, palms facing forward.
2. Curl the dumbbells up to your shoulders.
3. At the top, turn your wrists so your palms face down.
4. Lower slowly with your palms down, then turn them back up at the bottom.
• Use a weight you can lower slowly with the palms-down grip.\n• Keep your elbows by your sides throughout.

1. Sit on a bench with your forearms along your thighs, palms up, a dumbbell in each hand just past your knees.
2. Let the dumbbells roll down toward your fingertips.
3. Curl your wrists up as high as you can.
4. Lower slowly and repeat.
• Only your hands move; keep your forearms on your thighs.\n• Use a light weight and high reps.

1. Sit on a bench with your forearms along your thighs, palms down, a dumbbell in each hand just past your knees.
2. Let your hands drop as far as is comfortable.
3. Lift the backs of your hands up as high as you can.
4. Lower slowly and repeat.
• Use less weight than for the palms-up version.\n• Keep your forearms still on your thighs.

1. Sit on a bench with back support (or stand) and hold one dumbbell overhead with both hands, arms straight.
2. Keep your upper arms close to your head and pointing up.
3. Bend your elbows to lower the dumbbell behind your head until you feel a stretch in your triceps.
4. Straighten your arms to raise it back overhead.
• Don\'t let your elbows flare out; keep your upper arms still.\n• Brace your core so your lower back doesn\'t arch.

1. Place one knee and hand on a bench (or hinge forward), back flat, with a dumbbell in the other hand.
2. Raise that upper arm until it's parallel to the floor and close to your body, elbow bent at 90 degrees.
3. Straighten your arm back until it's fully extended.
4. Bend your elbow slowly to return; finish your reps and switch arms.
• Keep your upper arm fixed; only your forearm moves.\n• Use a light weight: swinging defeats the purpose.

1. Hold one dumbbell vertically against your chest, cupping the top end with both hands.
2. Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart or slightly wider, toes turned out a little.
3. Squat down between your knees, chest up, until your thighs are at least parallel.
4. Drive up through your whole foot to standing.
• Keep the dumbbell close to your chest and your elbows inside your knees.\n• Keep your heels down and your knees in line with your toes.

1. Stand with your feet wide and your toes turned out, holding one dumbbell upright by its top end between your legs.
2. Keep your chest up and your arms long.
3. Sit down between your feet, knees out over your toes, until your thighs are about parallel.
4. Drive up through your heels to standing.
• Push your knees out in line with your toes all the way down.\n• Keep your back upright; the dumbbell hangs straight down.

1. Stand about a stride in front of a bench, a dumbbell in each hand, and rest the top of your back foot on it.
2. Find a front-foot position where your knee bends comfortably and your heel stays down.
3. Lower your back knee toward the floor until your front thigh is about parallel to it.
4. Push through your front foot to rise; finish your reps, then switch legs.
• Keep your torso fairly upright and your front knee in line with your toes.\n• A longer stance works the glutes more; a shorter one, the quads.

1. Stand tall with a dumbbell in each hand at your sides, feet hip-width apart.
2. Step forward with one leg and lower your back knee toward the floor until both knees are bent about 90 degrees.
3. Push through your front foot to return to standing.
4. Alternate legs, or do all your reps on one side before switching.
• Keep your torso upright and your front knee in line with your toes.\n• Take a long enough step that your front heel stays on the floor.

1. Stand tall with a dumbbell in each hand at your sides.
2. Take a long step back and lower your back knee toward the floor.
3. Stop when your front thigh is about parallel, front knee over your foot.
4. Push through your front foot to bring your back leg forward to standing.
• Stepping back is easier on the knees than a forward lunge.\n• Keep your trunk upright and your front heel on the floor.

1. Stand with your feet wide, holding a dumbbell upright against your chest.
2. Shift your hips back and to one side, bending that knee while the other leg stays straight.
3. Go down until the bent thigh is about parallel, foot flat.
4. Push back to the middle and repeat to the other side.
• Keep both feet flat, pointing forward or slightly out.\n• You should feel a stretch on the inside of the straight leg.

1. Stand facing a sturdy box or bench about knee height, with a dumbbell in each hand.
2. Place one whole foot on the box.
3. Push through that foot to step up until your leg is straight, bringing the other foot up beside it.
4. Step down slowly, other foot first; finish your reps and switch legs.
• Drive with the leg on the box; don\'t push off with the back foot.\n• Use a stable box and keep your knee in line with your toes.

1. Stand tall with a dumbbell in each hand in front of your thighs, feet hip-width apart.
2. With your knees slightly bent and fixed, push your hips back and lower the dumbbells along your legs.
3. Go down until you feel a strong stretch in your hamstrings, back flat.
4. Drive your hips forward to stand up, squeezing your glutes.
• Keep the dumbbells close to your legs; your knees barely bend.\n• Keep your back neutral; stop when your hips can\'t go further back.

1. Stand on one leg with the knee soft, holding a dumbbell in the opposite hand.
2. Hinge forward at the hip, letting your free leg rise behind you in line with your body.
3. Lower the dumbbell toward the floor until your body is nearly horizontal, back flat.
4. Squeeze the glute of your standing leg to come back up; switch legs after the set.
• Keep your hips square to the floor: don\'t let the free hip open up.\n• Touch a wall or a bench with your free hand if you need balance.

1. Stand with the balls of your feet on a step, a dumbbell in each hand at your sides.
2. Lower your heels below the step as far as is comfortable.
3. Rise onto your toes as high as you can and hold for a moment.
4. Lower slowly and repeat.
• Keep your knees straight but not locked: only your ankles move.\n• Pause at the bottom instead of bouncing.

1. Sit on a bench with the balls of your feet on a step or plate and your knees bent at about 90 degrees.
2. Rest a dumbbell upright on each thigh, just above the knee, and hold it there.
3. Raise your heels as high as you can.
4. Lower them slowly below the step and repeat.
• With the knees bent it works the deeper calf muscle (soleus).\n• Use a full, slow range rather than heavy, bouncing reps.

1. Stand tall holding a dumbbell in one hand at your side, feet hip-width apart, the other hand on your waist.
2. Bend sideways toward the dumbbell, sliding it down your leg.
3. Return to upright by contracting the obliques on the opposite side.
4. Finish your reps and switch sides.
• Bend purely to the side; don\'t lean forward or twist.\n• Move slowly and use one dumbbell only: with two, one cancels out the other.

1. Stand with your feet a bit wider than hip-width, the kettlebell on the floor a short step in front of you.
2. Hinge at the hips, grip the handle with both hands and hike the bell back between your legs.
3. Snap your hips forward to swing it up to chest height, arms straight and relaxed.
4. Let it fall back between your legs, hinging at the hips, and flow into the next rep.
5. To stop, let it swing back once more and set it down in front of you.
• The power comes from your hips, not from your arms or a squat.\n• Keep your back flat and stand tall at the top; don\'t lean back.

1. Hold the kettlebell by the sides of the handle at your chest, elbows pointing down.
2. Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart or slightly wider, toes turned out a little.
3. Squat down between your knees, chest up, until your thighs are at least parallel.
4. Drive up through your whole foot to standing.
• Keep the kettlebell close to your chest and your elbows inside your knees.\n• Keep your heels down and your knees in line with your toes.

1. Stand with the kettlebell between your feet, hinge at the hips and grip the handle with one hand.
2. Drive your hips forward and pull the bell close to your body into the rack position at your shoulder.
3. Press it straight overhead until your arm is fully extended, biceps by your ear.
4. Lower it to your shoulder, then let it swing down between your legs, hinging, for the next rep.
5. Finish your reps and switch arms.
• Guide the bell close to your body so it doesn\'t flip over and hit your forearm.\n• Keep your wrist straight and squeeze your glutes as you press; don\'t lean back.

1. Lie on your back holding the kettlebell straight up in one hand; bend that knee, other arm and leg out wide.
2. Keeping your eyes on the bell, roll onto your opposite forearm, then push up onto that hand.
3. Lift your hips, sweep your straight leg back under you onto one knee and bring your torso upright.
4. Stand up from the kneeling position as if finishing a lunge, arm still straight overhead.
5. Reverse each step slowly to lie back down; finish your reps and switch sides.
• Keep the arm holding the bell straight and vertical the whole time, wrist straight.\n• Learn it with no weight or a very light one first; move slowly, one step at a time.

1. Stand with your feet a bit wider than hip-width and the kettlebell on the floor between your feet.
2. Push your hips back and bend your knees to grip the handle with both hands, back flat.
3. Stand up by driving your hips forward, the kettlebell close to your body.
4. Hinge back down and set it on the floor under control.
• Keep your chest up and your shoulders over the bell at the start.\n• The best way to learn the hip hinge before swings.

1. Stand with the kettlebell on the floor between your feet and grip it with one hand.
2. Hike it back between your legs, then drive your hips forward.
3. Keep the bell close and let it roll round your hand onto the back of your forearm at your shoulder (the rack).
4. Let it drop back between your legs and repeat; switch hands after the set.
• Guide the bell close to your body instead of swinging it out, so it doesn\'t bang your wrist.\n• In the rack, your elbow is tucked in and your wrist straight.

1. Clean the kettlebell to the rack position at your shoulder, elbow tucked in.
2. Brace your abs and glutes and stand tall.
3. Press the bell straight up until your arm is locked out beside your head.
4. Lower it back to the rack under control; switch arms after the set.
• Don\'t lean back or to the side; keep your ribs down.\n• Your forearm stays vertical under the bell all the way.

1. Hike the kettlebell back between your legs with one hand, back flat.
2. Snap your hips forward and pull the bell up close to your body.
3. As it passes your chest, punch your hand up so the bell rolls onto your forearm and your arm locks out overhead.
4. Let it drop back between your legs in one smooth arc; switch hands after the set.
• Learn the swing and the clean first, and start with a light bell.\n• Punch through at the top so the bell doesn\'t flip over and hit your forearm.

1. Put one knee and the same-side hand on a bench, back flat and parallel to the floor.
2. Hold the kettlebell in the other hand, arm hanging straight down.
3. Row it up to your hip, leading with your elbow.
4. Lower it slowly until your arm is straight; switch sides after the set.
• Keep your torso still; don\'t twist to lift it.\n• Pull toward your hip, not your shoulder.

1. Press a kettlebell overhead with one arm and turn your feet slightly away from it.
2. Keep your eyes on the bell and your arm vertical.
3. Push your hips out to the side of the bell and fold down, sliding your free hand down the inside of the other leg.
4. Go as low as you can with a straight back, then stand back up; switch sides after the set.
• Practise without weight, or with the bell held low, before going overhead.\n• The overhead arm stays locked and vertical the whole time.

1. Place your hands on the floor slightly wider than your shoulders, legs straight behind you, on your toes.
2. Brace your abs and glutes so your body forms a straight line from head to heels.
3. Lower your chest toward the floor by bending your elbows, keeping them at about 45 degrees.
4. Push back up until your arms are straight.
• Don\'t let your hips sag or pike up.\n• Too hard? Put your hands on a bench or do them from your knees.

1. Kneel on a mat with your hands on the floor, slightly wider than your shoulders.
2. Walk your hands forward until your body is straight from knees to head.
3. Lower your chest toward the floor, elbows at about 45 degrees from your body.
4. Push back up to straight arms.
• Keep your hips in line with your back; don\'t bend at the waist.\n• A good step toward full push-ups: move on when you can do 15 to 20.

1. Place your hands on the edge of a bench or box, slightly wider than your shoulders.
2. Step back until your body is straight from head to heels.
3. Lower your chest to the edge, elbows at about 45 degrees.
4. Push back up to straight arms.
• The higher the support, the easier: lower it as you get stronger.\n• Keep your body in one straight line.

1. Put your feet on a bench behind you and your hands on the floor, slightly wider than your shoulders.
2. Brace so your body is straight from head to heels.
3. Lower your chest toward the floor, elbows at about 45 degrees.
4. Push back up to straight arms.
• Raising the feet shifts more work to the upper chest and shoulders.\n• Don\'t let your hips sag or your head drop.

1. Get into a push-up position with your hands together under your chest, thumbs and index fingers forming a diamond.
2. Keep your body straight from head to heels.
3. Lower your chest to your hands, elbows close to your sides.
4. Push back up to straight arms.
• Your elbows go back along your body, not out to the sides.\n• Harder than a regular push-up: do them on your knees if needed.

1. Start in a push-up position and walk your feet in, lifting your hips high so your body forms an upside-down V.
2. Hands shoulder-width apart, arms and back in a straight line.
3. Bend your elbows to lower the top of your head toward the floor between your hands.
4. Press back up to straight arms.
• The higher your hips, the more your shoulders work.\n• Feet on a box make it harder: a step toward handstand push-ups.

1. Grip the parallel bars and jump or step up until your arms are straight, shoulders over your hands.
2. Bend your knees or keep your legs straight below you, and brace your core.
3. Lower yourself by bending your elbows until your upper arms are about parallel to the floor.
4. Push back up until your arms are straight.
• Keep your shoulders down, away from your ears, and don\'t go deeper than is comfortable.\n• Lean slightly forward for more chest; stay upright for more triceps.

1. Sit on the edge of a bench, hands beside your hips gripping the edge, fingers forward.
2. Slide your hips off the bench, legs bent (easier) or straight (harder).
3. Bend your elbows to lower your hips until your upper arms are about parallel to the floor.
4. Push through your hands to straighten your arms.
• Keep your back close to the bench and your elbows pointing back, not out.\n• Don\'t go too low; stop if your shoulders feel strained.

1. Grip the bar slightly wider than your shoulders, palms facing away, and hang with your arms straight.
2. Pull your shoulders down and brace your core, legs still.
3. Pull yourself up until your chin is above the bar, driving your elbows down.
4. Lower slowly until your arms are straight again.
• Don\'t swing or kick to get up; keep the movement controlled.\n• Can\'t do one yet? Use the assisted machine, a band or slow lowerings from the top.

1. Grip the bar shoulder-width apart with your palms facing you and hang with your arms straight.
2. Pull your shoulders down and brace your core.
3. Pull yourself up until your chin is above the bar, keeping your elbows in front of you.
4. Lower slowly until your arms are straight.
• Avoid swinging; keep your legs still.\n• Use the full range: start every rep from straight arms.

1. Set a bar in a rack or Smith machine at about waist height and lie underneath it.
2. Grip the bar slightly wider than your shoulders and hang with straight arms, heels down and body straight.
3. Pull your chest up to the bar, squeezing your shoulder blades together.
4. Lower slowly until your arms are straight.
• Keep your body in a straight line from head to heels; don\'t let your hips sag.\n• Bend your knees to make it easier; a lower bar makes it harder.

1. Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart, toes turned out slightly, arms in front of you for balance.
2. Push your hips back and bend your knees to squat down, chest up.
3. Go as low as you can with your heels down and back neutral, ideally to parallel or below.
4. Push through your whole foot to stand back up.
• Keep your knees in line with your toes; don\'t let them cave in.\n• Keep your weight over your mid-foot, heels on the floor.

1. Stand tall with your feet hip-width apart and your hands on your hips.
2. Step forward with one leg and lower your back knee toward the floor until both knees are bent about 90 degrees.
3. Push through your front foot to return to standing.
4. Alternate legs, or do all your reps on one side before switching.
• Keep your torso upright and your front knee in line with your toes.\n• Take a long enough step that your front heel stays down.

1. Stand on one leg with the other leg straight out in front and your arms forward for balance.
2. Sit down slowly on the standing leg, keeping the heel on the floor.
3. Go as low as you can control, the free leg off the floor.
4. Drive back up to standing; switch legs after the set.
• Start by sitting down onto a bench or holding a post until you have the strength.\n• Keep your knee in line with your toes.

1. Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart.
2. Squat down quickly, swinging your arms back.
3. Jump up as high as you can, swinging your arms up.
4. Land softly on the balls of your feet, bend your knees to absorb it and go into the next rep.
• Land quietly with your knees in line with your toes.\n• Quality over quantity: stop when your jumps get lower.

1. Stand with your feet very wide, toes slightly out.
2. Shift your weight to one side and sit down deep over that foot, keeping the heel down.
3. Let the other leg straighten with its toes turning up.
4. Push back to the middle and go to the other side.
• Go only as deep as your hips allow; hold onto something at first.\n• Keep your chest up and your bent knee over your toes.

1. Stand on one foot on the edge of a step, heel hanging off, holding a wall or post for balance.
2. Hook the other foot behind your ankle.
3. Rise onto your toes as high as you can, then lower your heel slowly below the step.
4. Finish the set and switch feet.
• Keep your knee straight but not locked.\n• Hold a dumbbell in your free hand when it gets easy.

1. Lie on your back with your knees bent, feet flat on the floor hip-width apart, arms at your sides.
2. Brace your core and press your lower back gently toward the floor.
3. Drive through your heels to lift your hips until your knees, hips and shoulders are in line.
4. Squeeze your glutes at the top, then lower slowly.
• Don\'t arch your lower back at the top; the lift comes from your glutes.\n• Make it harder on one leg or with a pause at the top.

1. Lie on your back with one knee bent and that foot flat, the other leg straight in the air.
2. Arms by your sides, palms down.
3. Push through your heel to lift your hips until your body is straight from shoulders to knee.
4. Lower slowly; switch legs after the set.
• Keep your hips level: don\'t let the free side drop.\n• Squeeze your glute at the top for a second.

1. Get on all fours with your hands under your shoulders and your knees under your hips.
2. Keeping one knee bent at 90 degrees, push that foot up toward the ceiling.
3. Stop when your thigh is in line with your back.
4. Lower the knee without touching the floor; switch legs after the set.
• Don\'t arch your lower back: the movement comes from the hip.\n• Add an ankle weight or a band when it gets easy.

1. Set the pad just below your hip bones and hook your heels under the foot rollers.
2. Cross your arms on your chest (or hold a plate), body in a straight line.
3. Bend forward at the hips with a flat back until you feel a stretch in your hamstrings.
4. Raise your torso until your body is in line with your legs again.
• Stop when your body is straight; don\'t swing up into an arch.\n• Move slowly and keep your neck neutral.

1. Lie face down with your arms stretched out in front and your legs straight.
2. Squeeze your glutes and lift your arms, chest and legs off the floor together.
3. Hold for a moment, looking at the floor.
4. Lower slowly and repeat.
• Lift only a few centimetres: control matters, not height.\n• Keep your neck in line; don\'t look up.

1. Get on all fours with your hands under your shoulders and your knees under your hips.
2. Brace your abs to keep your back flat.
3. Reach one arm forward and the opposite leg back until both are level with your body.
4. Hold for a moment, return slowly and switch sides.
• Keep your hips level, as if balancing a glass on your lower back.\n• Move slowly; reach long rather than high.

1. Kneel on a pad with your ankles anchored under a bench or roller, or held by a partner.
2. Keep your body straight from knees to shoulders, hands ready in front of your chest.
3. Lower yourself forward as slowly as you can, resisting with your hamstrings.
4. Catch yourself with your hands at the bottom and push lightly back up to the start.
• Keep your hips straight; don\'t bend at the waist to make it easier.\n• Focus on the slow lowering; use your hands as much as you need on the way up.

1. Lie on your back with your knees bent and feet flat, hands lightly behind your head or crossed on your chest.
2. Brace your abs and press your lower back toward the floor.
3. Breathing out, curl your head, shoulders and upper back off the floor, bringing your ribs toward your hips.
4. Lower slowly back down.
• Don\'t pull on your neck; keep a fist\'s space between your chin and chest.\n• It\'s a short movement: your lower back stays on the floor.

1. Lie on your back with your knees bent and feet flat (anchored if needed), arms crossed on your chest.
2. Brace your abs.
3. Curl up through your spine until your torso is upright, breathing out as you rise.
4. Lower slowly back down, one vertebra at a time.
• Don\'t yank yourself up with your arms or neck.\n• Lower under control rather than dropping back.

1. Hang from a pull-up bar with your arms straight and hands shoulder-width apart.
2. Pull your shoulders down slightly and keep your legs together and still.
3. Raise your legs, straight or with knees bent, until your thighs pass parallel, tilting your pelvis up.
4. Lower them slowly without swinging.
• Avoid swinging: pause at the bottom between reps.\n• Tilt your pelvis up at the top so your abs, not just your hip flexors, do the work.

1. Hang from a pull-up bar with your arms straight and your legs together.
2. Brace your abs and stop any swinging.
3. Bring your knees up toward your chest, curling your hips up at the top.
4. Lower your legs slowly to the start.
• Avoid swinging: pause at the bottom if you start to sway.\n• An easier step toward the straight-leg hanging leg raise.

1. Lie on your back with your legs straight and your hands under your hips or at your sides.
2. Press your lower back into the floor and brace your abs.
3. Raise your legs together until they're vertical.
4. Lower them slowly, stopping before your lower back lifts off the floor.
• Your lower back must stay on the floor; bend your knees if it lifts.\n• Move slowly; don\'t let your legs drop.

1. Lie on your back with your hands by your sides and your knees bent at 90 degrees, thighs vertical.
2. Brace your abs and press your lower back into the floor.
3. Curl your hips off the floor, bringing your knees toward your chest.
4. Lower your hips slowly back to the floor.
• Lift with your abs, not by swinging your legs.\n• Keep the movement small and slow.

1. Lie on your back with your hands behind your head and your shoulders lifted off the floor.
2. Lift your legs with your knees bent.
3. Bring one knee in while you turn the opposite elbow toward it, straightening the other leg.
4. Switch sides in a steady pedalling motion.
• Turn your shoulders, not just your elbows; don\'t pull on your neck.\n• Slow and controlled works better than fast.

1. Lie on your back with your arms pointing at the ceiling and your knees bent at 90 degrees over your hips.
2. Press your lower back into the floor.
3. Lower one arm overhead and straighten the opposite leg toward the floor, without touching it.
4. Return and switch sides.
• Your lower back stays on the floor: move only as far as you can keep it there.\n• Breathe out as you extend.

1. Lie on a bench and grip it behind your head.
2. Lift your hips and legs until your body is straight and almost vertical, resting on your upper back.
3. Lower your body as one straight line, as slowly as you can, until it's just above the bench.
4. Raise it back up and repeat.
• An advanced exercise: start with your knees bent or with the lowering only.\n• Don\'t bend at the hips; your body stays straight from shoulders to toes.

1. Sit on the floor with your knees bent and heels down (or lifted to make it harder).
2. Lean back with a straight back until you feel your abs working, hands together or holding a weight.
3. Rotate your torso to one side, bringing your hands toward the floor beside your hip.
4. Rotate to the other side and keep alternating with control.
• Turn from your ribs and shoulders, not just your arms.\n• Keep your back straight; don\'t slump.

1. Start in a high plank: hands under your shoulders, body straight from head to heels.
2. Drive one knee toward your chest.
3. Switch legs quickly, bringing the other knee in as the first foot goes back.
4. Keep alternating at a steady pace.
• Keep your hips level and low; your shoulders stay over your hands.\n• Brace your abs and breathe steadily.

1. Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart, then squat down and place your hands on the floor.
2. Jump or step your feet back into a plank.
3. Do a push-up (optional), then jump or step your feet back toward your hands.
4. Stand up and jump, reaching your arms overhead; land softly and go into the next rep.
• Keep your body straight in the plank; don\'t let your hips sag.\n• Step instead of jumping to make it easier; land with soft knees.

1. Lie on your back on a bench with your head and neck past its end.
2. Hold a light plate on your forehead, or use no weight at first.
3. Let your head go back slowly, then bring your chin toward your chest.
4. Return to neutral and repeat.
• Use very light weight and slow, smooth reps; never jerk your neck.\n• Stay within a comfortable range.

1. Lie face down on a bench with your head and neck past its end, holding the bench.
2. Let your head drop slowly toward the floor.
3. Raise your head until you look forward, without arching your back.
4. Lower slowly and repeat.
• Start with no weight; later you can hold a light plate on the back of your head.\n• Slow, smooth reps in a comfortable range.

1. Lie on your side on a bench with your head past its end.
2. Let your head drop slowly toward the floor.
3. Raise your ear toward your top shoulder, keeping your face forward.
4. Lower slowly; switch sides after the set.
• No weight to start; later, a light plate held on the side of your head.\n• Move slowly and never force the end of the range.

1. Place your forearms on the floor with your elbows under your shoulders.
2. Step your feet back onto your toes so your body is straight from head to heels.
3. Brace your abs and squeeze your glutes.
4. Hold the position for your target time, then lower your knees to rest.
• Breathe steadily; don\'t hold your breath.\n• Keep your hips in line, neither sagging nor piked; look at the floor to keep your neck neutral.

1. Lie on your side with your elbow under your shoulder and your legs straight, feet stacked.
2. Lift your hips until your body is straight from head to feet.
3. Hold the position, hips high, top hand on your hip or pointing up.
4. Lower your hips, then repeat on the other side.
• Breathe steadily throughout the hold.\n• Don\'t let your hips sag or rotate forward; bend your bottom knee to make it easier.

1. Lie on your side next to a bench, elbow under your shoulder, and rest your top leg on the bench (knee or ankle).
2. Lift your hips so your body is straight, supported by your forearm and your top leg.
3. Bring your bottom leg up toward the bench, or let it hang, and hold.
4. Lower down, then repeat on the other side.
• Resting your knee on the bench is easier than your ankle: start there.\n• Keep your hips high and in line, and breathe steadily.

1. Stand with your back against a wall and your feet about a step in front of you, hip-width apart.
2. Slide down the wall until your knees are bent about 90 degrees, thighs parallel to the floor.
3. Keep your back flat against the wall and hold, hands off your thighs.
4. Slide back up the wall to finish.
• Keep your knees over your ankles, not past your toes.\n• Breathe steadily; stay higher on the wall if 90 degrees is too hard.

1. Grip a pull-up bar with your palms facing away, hands shoulder-width apart.
2. Lift your feet and hang with your arms straight.
3. Keep your shoulders slightly engaged (not shrugged up to your ears) and your body still.
4. Hold for your target time, then step down carefully.
• Breathe steadily and relax your legs.\n• Use a box or step to reach the bar and to get down; don\'t drop from a height.

1. Lie on your back with your arms overhead and your legs straight.
2. Press your lower back into the floor.
3. Lift your shoulders and legs a little off the floor, your body in a shallow banana shape.
4. Hold for your target time, breathing steadily.
• If your lower back lifts, bend your knees or bring your arms to your sides.\n• Keep your chin slightly tucked.

1. Place your hands on parallettes, dip bars or two benches beside your hips.
2. Press down to straighten your arms and lift your body.
3. Raise your legs straight out in front until they're level with your hips.
4. Hold for your target time, then lower your feet.
• Push your shoulders down, away from your ears.\n• Start with your knees bent (tuck) and straighten them as you get stronger.

1. Sit or stand tall and place your palms on your forehead.
2. Press your head into your hands while your hands resist, so nothing moves.
3. Hold for your target time, breathing steadily.
4. Repeat with a hand on the side of your head, then on the back of your head.
• Build up the pressure gradually and never push into pain.\n• Keep your head neutral, chin level.

1. Stand between two heavy dumbbells, squat down with a flat back and grip one in each hand.
2. Stand up tall, shoulders back and down, arms straight at your sides.
3. Walk with short, controlled steps for your target time or distance.
4. Stop, then squat down with a flat back to set the dumbbells on the floor.
• Keep your torso upright; don\'t lean to either side.\n• Breathe steadily and squeeze the handles hard.

1. Hold a heavy dumbbell or kettlebell in one hand at your side.
2. Stand tall with your shoulders level.
3. Walk with short, steady steps for your target time without leaning toward the weight.
4. Set it down carefully and repeat with the other hand.
• Your trunk works to keep you straight: don\'t tilt.\n• Keep your free arm relaxed and your grip tight.

1. Stand tall holding a light band in front of you at shoulder height, hands shoulder-width apart, palms down.
2. Keep your arms straight with a slight bend in your elbows.
3. Pull the band apart by moving your hands out to the sides until it touches your chest.
4. Return slowly, keeping tension on the band.
• Keep your shoulders down and your ribs in; don\'t arch your back.\n• Choose a band that lets you complete the full range; hands closer together make it harder.

1. Place a mini band around your legs, just above your knees or around your ankles.
