2. Stand with your feet hip-width apart and sink into a quarter squat, chest up.
3. Step sideways with one foot, keeping tension on the band, then follow with the other without your feet touching.
4. Take your planned number of steps, then walk back the other way.
• Keep your knees pushed out and your toes pointing forward.\n• Stay low at the same height; don\'t bob up and down or sway your torso.

1. Anchor a band behind you at chest height and hold one handle in each hand.
2. Step forward into a split stance until the band is tight, hands beside your chest.
3. Press your hands forward until your arms are straight.
4. Return slowly to your chest.
• Keep your elbows slightly below shoulder height.\n• Step farther from the anchor to make it harder.

1. Anchor a band in front of you at chest height and hold the ends.
2. Step back until it's tight, knees soft and back straight.
3. Pull your hands to your lower ribs, squeezing your shoulder blades together.
4. Return slowly until your arms are straight.
• Lead with your elbows and keep your shoulders down.\n• Pause for a second at your ribs.

1. Anchor a band at head height and hold the ends with your palms facing down.
2. Step back until it's tight, arms straight in front of you.
3. Pull the band toward your face with your elbows high and wide, hands ending beside your ears.
4. Return slowly to straight arms.
• Squeeze your shoulder blades and rotate your hands back at the end.\n• Keep your ribs down; don\'t lean back.

1. Stand on the middle of a band and hold one end in each hand at your sides.
2. Keep a slight bend in your elbows.
3. Raise your arms out to the sides up to shoulder height.
4. Lower slowly, keeping tension on the band.
• Lead with your elbows and don\'t shrug.\n• Stand with your feet wider apart on the band for more tension.

1. Anchor a band at elbow height and stand side-on to it, holding it with the hand farthest from the anchor.
2. Keep that elbow against your side, bent at 90 degrees, forearm across your belly.
3. Rotate your forearm outward, away from your body, keeping the elbow in place.
4. Return slowly; switch sides after the set.
• A rolled towel between your elbow and your side helps keep it in.\n• Use a light band: this works the small rotator cuff muscles.

1. Stand on the middle of a band and hold one end in each hand, palms forward.
2. Keep your elbows by your sides.
3. Curl your hands up to your shoulders.
4. Lower slowly until your arms are straight.
• The band is hardest near the top: squeeze there for a moment.\n• Keep your elbows still and don\'t lean back.

1. Anchor a band high, above head height, and hold the ends.
2. Stand facing it with your elbows by your sides, bent.
3. Push your hands down until your arms are straight.
4. Let them come back up slowly to about chest height.
• Only your forearms move; keep your elbows pinned.\n• Step back from the anchor for more tension.

1. Stand on a band with your feet hip-width apart, loop the other end behind your neck and hold it at your shoulders.
2. Stand tall with your knees soft.
3. Hinge forward at the hips with a flat back until you feel a stretch in your hamstrings.
4. Drive your hips forward to stand back up.
• Push your hips back rather than bending down.\n• Keep the band on your upper back, not on the bones of your neck.

1. Lie on your back and loop a strap or towel round one foot.
2. Raise that leg straight up, the other leg flat on the floor.
3. Draw the leg gently toward you until you feel a stretch behind the thigh.
4. Hold, breathing slowly, then switch legs.
• Keep the raised knee almost straight and your hips on the floor.\n• A gentle stretch, never pain; ease a little further each time you breathe out.

1. Kneel on one knee on a mat, the other foot flat in front with the knee bent.
2. Tuck your pelvis under and squeeze the glute of the kneeling leg.
3. Shift your hips forward until you feel a stretch at the front of the back hip.
4. Hold, breathing slowly, then switch sides.
• Keep your trunk upright; don\'t arch your lower back.\n• Raise the arm on the kneeling side for a deeper stretch.

1. Kneel with your back to a bench or sofa, one knee on the floor against it and that shin up its front.
2. Step the other foot forward, knee bent at 90 degrees.
3. Tuck your pelvis under and bring your trunk upright until you feel a stretch at the front of the back thigh.
4. Hold, breathing slowly, then switch sides.
• It\'s intense: start with the knee farther from the bench and your trunk leaning forward.\n• Pad the knee with a cushion or a folded mat.

1. From all fours, bring one knee forward behind your wrist with the shin across the front of your body.
2. Slide the other leg straight back.
3. Lower your hips and fold forward onto your forearms until you feel a stretch in the front leg's glute.
4. Hold, breathing slowly, then switch sides.
• Keep your hips square; put a cushion under the front hip if it doesn\'t reach the floor.\n• Bring the front foot closer to your hips if your knee feels any strain.

1. Sit on the floor with the soles of your feet together and your knees out to the sides.
2. Hold your feet and sit tall.
3. Lean forward from the hips with a long back until you feel a stretch in your inner thighs.
4. Hold, breathing slowly.
• Bring your feet closer to you for a deeper stretch.\n• Let your knees drop on their own; don\'t push them down.

1. Step into a long lunge and lower your back knee to the floor.
2. Put the hand on the back leg's side on the floor inside your front foot.
3. Reach the other arm up to the ceiling, opening your chest, and follow your hand with your eyes.
4. Bring the arm back down, repeat a few times and switch sides.
• Keep your hips low and your front knee over your foot.\n• Breathe out as you rotate; move slowly.

1. Stand facing a wall with your hands on it at shoulder height.
2. Step one foot back, keeping that leg straight and the heel on the floor.
3. Bend your front knee and lean toward the wall until you feel a stretch in the back calf.
4. Hold, breathing slowly, then switch legs.
• Keep the back foot pointing straight ahead.\n• Bend the back knee slightly to stretch the lower calf (soleus).

1. Get on all fours with your hands under your shoulders and your knees under your hips.
2. Breathe out and round your back up toward the ceiling, tucking your chin and pelvis (cat).
3. Breathe in and let your belly drop, lifting your chest and tailbone (cow).
4. Keep moving slowly between the two for your target time.
• Move one vertebra at a time, in time with your breathing.\n• Keep your arms straight; the movement is in your spine.

1. Kneel on a mat with your big toes together and your knees about hip-width apart.
2. Sit your hips back toward your heels.
3. Fold forward and rest your forehead on the floor, arms stretched out in front.
4. Hold, breathing slowly into your back.
• Put a cushion between your hips and heels if they don\'t reach.\n• Walk your hands to one side to stretch the opposite side of your back.

1. Get on all fours and put one hand behind your head.
2. Turn that elbow down toward the opposite wrist.
3. Then turn it up toward the ceiling as far as you can, following it with your eyes.
4. Repeat slowly for your target time, then switch sides.
• Keep your hips still: the turn comes from your upper back.\n• Breathe out as you open up.

1. Stand in a doorway and place one forearm on the frame, elbow at shoulder height and bent at 90 degrees.
2. Step forward with the foot on the same side.
3. Lean gently through the doorway until you feel a stretch across your chest.
4. Hold, breathing slowly, then switch sides.
• Keep your shoulder down and back; don\'t let it roll forward.\n• Raise or lower the elbow to stretch different parts of the chest.

1. Stand or sit tall and bring one arm straight across your chest.
2. Hook your other forearm over it, just above the elbow.
3. Gently draw the arm closer to your chest until you feel a stretch at the back of the shoulder.
4. Hold, breathing slowly, then switch sides.
• Keep the shoulder of the stretched arm down, away from your ear.\n• Pull on the upper arm, not on the elbow joint.

1. Stand or sit tall and raise one arm overhead.
2. Bend that elbow so your hand drops behind your head toward your upper back.
3. With your other hand, gently ease the elbow back until you feel a stretch along the back of the arm.
4. Hold, breathing slowly, then switch sides.
• Keep your head up; don\'t let the arm push it forward.\n• Keep your ribs down rather than arching your back.

1. Hold a light band (or a stick) in front of your hips with a wide grip, arms straight.
2. Raise it over your head, keeping your arms straight.
3. Carry on down behind your back as far as is comfortable.
4. Bring it back the same way, slowly, for your target time.
• Use a grip wide enough to pass without bending your elbows; narrow it as you gain mobility.\n• Move slowly and stop if you feel any pinching.

1. Sit tall and hold the side of your seat with one hand.
2. Bring the other hand over your head to the opposite side.
3. Gently tilt your ear toward your shoulder until you feel a stretch along the side of your neck.
4. Hold, breathing slowly, then switch sides.
• The hand only adds a little weight; don\'t pull hard.\n• Keep both shoulders down and your face looking forward.

1. Stand on the side rails, clip the safety key to your clothes and start the belt at a slow speed.
2. Step onto the belt and walk for a few minutes to warm up.
3. Raise the speed or incline gradually to your target effort.
4. To finish, slow down for a few minutes before stopping the belt and stepping off.

• Don\'t hold the handrails while you walk or run: it changes your posture and the effort.\n• Stay near the front of the belt, look ahead and keep your strides natural.\n• For a harder walk, add incline instead of very high speeds.

1. Set the seat so your knee is slightly bent when the pedal is at the bottom.
2. Set the handlebar at a comfortable height and fasten the pedal straps if there are any.
3. Start pedalling at a light resistance for a few minutes to warm up.
4. Raise the resistance or cadence to your target effort, and lower it again for the last minutes.
• A good starting point: the seat at hip height when you stand next to the bike.\n• Keep your back straight and your knees in line with your feet, not pointing out.

1. Set the saddle at about hip height so your knee is slightly bent at the bottom of the pedal stroke.
2. Adjust the saddle fore and aft and the handlebar height, then secure your feet in the pedals or clips.
3. Warm up for a few minutes at a light resistance.
4. Vary resistance and cadence, seated or standing, and ease off for the last few minutes.
• The flywheel keeps the pedals turning: use the brake to stop and don\'t take your feet out while it spins.\n• Always keep some resistance on, especially when you pedal standing.

1. Slide the seat so your knee is slightly bent when the pedal is at its farthest point.
2. Sit with your back against the backrest and fasten the pedal straps.
3. Start pedalling at a light resistance for a few minutes to warm up.
4. Raise the resistance or cadence to your target effort, and lower it again for the last minutes.
• Keep your back against the backrest and your knees in line with your feet.\n• Don\'t lock your knees at full extension; move the seat closer if they do.

1. Set the seat so your knee is slightly bent when the pedal is at the bottom.
2. Grip the moving handles and place your feet on the pedals.
3. Push and pull the handles as you pedal; the faster you go, the more the fan resists.
4. Warm up gently, then work at your target effort; slow down gradually to finish.
• The resistance rises steeply with speed: pace yourself on longer efforts.\n• Use your arms and legs together and keep your torso stable.

1. Step onto the pedals holding the handles and start moving slowly.
2. Set the resistance and incline (if there is one) for a light warm-up.
3. Push and pull the moving handles as you stride, or hold the fixed ones to focus on your legs.
4. Raise the resistance to your target effort, then ease off for the last few minutes.
• Stand tall and keep your whole foot on the pedals; don\'t lean on the handles.\n• Pedal backwards now and then for variety.

1. Strap your feet in across the widest part of the foot and set the damper (3 to 5 is a good start).
2. Sit tall and grip the handle with your arms straight and your shins vertical.
3. Push with your legs first, then lean back slightly and pull the handle to your lower ribs.
4. Return in reverse: arms forward, lean forward from the hips, then bend your knees to slide in.

• Drive: legs, body, arms. Return: arms, body, legs.\n• Keep your back straight and don\'t pull with your arms before your legs are almost straight.\n• A higher damper isn\'t more effort by itself; the power comes from the leg drive.

1. Step onto the stairs holding the side rails and start at a slow speed.
2. Climb with your whole foot on each step, standing tall.
3. Raise the speed gradually to your target effort.
4. Slow down for the last few minutes, then wait for the stairs to stop before stepping off.
• Use the rails only for balance; don\'t lean on them or hang your weight on your arms.\n• Keep your torso upright rather than hunched over the console.

1. Stand facing the machine, feet hip-width apart, set the damper and grip the handles overhead.
2. Pull the handles down, hinging at the hips and bending your knees slightly, like a double-pole ski stroke.
3. Finish with your hands past your hips and your torso leaning forward.
4. Stand back up and let your arms rise with the handles to start the next pull.
• Use your whole body: your core and hips drive the pull, not just your arms.\n• Keep your back flat as you hinge; don\'t turn it into a squat.

1. Warm up for 10 minutes: easy jogging, leg swings, side steps and a few short sprints.
2. Stay on the balls of your feet with your knees soft, so you can turn and stop quickly.
3. Pass with the inside of your foot for accuracy and strike with your laces for power, your standing foot beside the ball.
4. In Fortia, log the time you played, for example 1:30:00, and the calories if your watch shows them.

• Cool down by walking for a few minutes, then stretch your calves, hamstrings and hip flexors.\n• Drink at every break, more on hot days.\n• Wear boots with studs that suit the pitch: natural grass, artificial turf or indoor.

1. Warm up for 10 minutes: jogging, side shuffles, leg swings and quick changes of direction.
2. Control the ball with the sole of your foot: the smaller, heavier ball stays close and barely bounces.
3. Keep moving to offer passes in the small space, and shoot early with your toe or laces.
4. In Fortia, log the time you played, for example 1:00:00, and the calories if your watch shows them.
• Use flat indoor shoes with non-marking soles, never studs.\n• The court is hard: land softly and warm up your ankles and knees well.

1. Warm up for 10 minutes: jogging, side shuffles, a few jumps and easy shots close to the basket.
2. Dribble with your fingertips, not your palm, keeping the ball at hip height and your eyes up.
3. Shoot with your elbow under the ball, push up with your legs and flick your wrist at the end.
4. In Fortia, log the time you played, for example 1:00:00, and the calories if your watch shows them.
• Land from jumps on both feet with your knees bent, not stiff.\n• Wear basketball shoes with good grip and ankle support.

1. Warm up for 10 minutes: jogging, arm circles, squats and some easy passing in pairs.
2. To pass, bend your knees and join your forearms into a flat platform; move your feet, not your arms.
3. To spike, take a two- or three-step approach, jump off both feet and hit the ball at its highest point.
4. In Fortia, log the time you played, for example 1:30:00, and the calories if your watch shows them.
• Land from every jump on both feet, knees bent and in line with your toes.\n• On sand, play barefoot or in sand socks and warm up your calves and ankles well.

1. Warm up for 10 minutes: jogging, arm circles, side shuffles and easy passes.
2. Throw with your elbow at shoulder height or above, stepping forward with the foot opposite your throwing arm.
3. Take at most three steps with the ball, then pass, shoot or bounce it.
4. In Fortia, log the time you played, for example 1:00:00, and the calories if your watch shows them.
• Warm up your shoulder with light throws before shooting hard.\n• Land from jump shots on both feet when you can, with your knees bent.

1. Warm up for 10 minutes: jogging, arm circles, side steps and a few gentle rallies from the service line.
2. Wait in the ready position: feet apart, knees bent, racket in front, weight on the balls of your feet.
3. Turn your shoulders early and swing from low to high, letting your hips and trunk drive the stroke.
4. In Fortia, log the time you played, for example 1:30:00, and the calories if your watch shows them.
• Hit with a relaxed grip: squeezing the racket tires your forearm and can lead to tennis elbow.\n• After every shot, step back to your position near the middle of the baseline.

1. Warm up for 10 minutes: jogging, arm circles, side steps and a few volleys at the net.
2. Hold the racket in front of you with your elbow slightly bent, and keep your strokes short and controlled.
3. Let the ball come off the back glass before you hit it, and use lobs to win the net.
4. In Fortia, log the time you played, for example 1:30:00, and the calories if your watch shows them.
• Move as a pair: go up to the net and back together with your partner.\n• Wear padel or tennis shoes with a herringbone sole for the sand on the court.

1. Warm up for 10 minutes: skipping, side shuffles, lunges and arm circles.
2. Hold the racket loosely, as if shaking hands, and wait in the middle of the court with your knees bent.
3. Hit overhead shots high and in front of you, turning your forearm and snapping your wrist at contact.
4. In Fortia, log the time you played, for example 1:00:00, and the calories if your watch shows them.
• When you lunge for the shuttle, keep your knee over your foot, not past it, and push back to the middle.\n• Wear indoor court shoes: running shoes grip poorly and make it easier to roll an ankle.

1. Start at an easy pace for 5 minutes to warm up.
2. Walk tall, looking ahead, with your arms swinging naturally and your heel landing first.
3. Pick up the pace until you breathe faster but can still talk.
4. In Fortia, log the time and the distance in km (your phone or watch shows it), for example 45:00 and 4.5 km.
• Short, quick steps are faster and easier on your joints than long strides.\n• Wear comfortable, cushioned shoes, and add hills or stairs for a harder walk.

1. Start slowly on the first, easier stretch so your legs and breathing warm up.
2. Uphill, take shorter steps and lean slightly forward from the ankles; push with the poles if you use them.
3. Downhill, bend your knees, keep your steps short and look a few metres ahead.
4. In Fortia, log the time and the distance in km, for example 3:00:00 and 12 km.
• Carry water, a snack and an extra layer, and tell someone your route.\n• Boots with a grippy sole and ankle support help on rough or wet ground.

1. Warm up with 5 to 10 minutes of brisk walking or very easy jogging.
2. Run tall with a slight forward lean, landing softly under your body, not far in front of it.
3. Keep your arms bent at about 90° and relaxed, swinging forward and back, not across your body.
4. In Fortia, log the time and the distance in km, for example 30:00 and 5 km.
• Most runs should be easy enough to hold a conversation; increase your weekly distance gradually.\n• Finish with a few minutes of walking and stretch your calves, hamstrings and quads.

1. Check the tyres, the brakes and your helmet, and set the saddle so your knee is only slightly bent at the bottom of the pedal stroke.
2. Ride easily in a light gear for the first 10 minutes.
3. Pedal smoothly in circles at a brisk cadence, and change down before climbs.
4. In Fortia, log the time and the distance in km, for example 1:30:00 and 40 km.
• Ride predictably: signal your turns and use lights when the light is poor.\n• Hold the bars with a relaxed grip and your elbows slightly bent to absorb bumps.

1. Warm up with a few easy lengths in any stroke.
2. In front crawl, keep your body long and flat with your face in the water, and kick from the hips with nearly straight legs.
3. Reach forward with each arm, pull back under your body and turn your head to the side to breathe.
4. In Fortia, log the time and the distance in km, for example 40:00 and 1.5 km (60 lengths of 25 m).
• Breathe out slowly underwater, so you only need to breathe in when you turn your head.\n• Swim easy lengths between the hard ones instead of stopping for long.

1. Start with a few minutes of slow breathing and gentle movements, like cat-cow.
2. Move into each pose slowly with your breath: inhale to lengthen, exhale to fold or twist.
3. Hold each pose for a few breaths without pain; use blocks or bend your knees when you need to.
4. In Fortia, log the time of the session, for example 1:00:00.
• Keep breathing through your nose: if you hold your breath, the pose is too hard for now.\n• Stretch to a mild pull, never to sharp pain.

1. Lie on your back on a mat, find a neutral spine and breathe into your ribs.
2. Before every movement, gently draw your navel in and keep your core engaged.
3. Move slowly and with control, one vertebra at a time in rolling exercises such as the roll-up.
4. In Fortia, log the time of the session, for example 50:00.
• Quality beats quantity: a few precise repetitions are better than many sloppy ones.\n• Keep your neck long and relaxed; if it strains, rest your head on the mat.

1. Warm up for 5 to 10 minutes with easy steps and shoulder and hip circles.
2. Learn each step slowly first, then bring it up to the speed of the music.
3. Stay light on the balls of your feet with your knees soft, and let your arms follow the rhythm.
4. In Fortia, log the time you danced, for example 1:00:00, and the calories if your watch shows them.
• Drink water between songs and rest when you need to.\n• Wear shoes that suit the floor and the style: they should let you turn without sticking.

1. Warm up for 10 minutes: skipping rope, shadow boxing and shoulder circles.
2. Stand side-on with your lead foot forward, knees soft, hands up by your chin and elbows in.
3. Jab by shooting the lead arm straight out and back; throw the cross by turning your rear hip and foot.
4. In Fortia, log the time of the session, for example 1:00:00, and the calories if your watch shows them.
• Breathe out with every punch and bring your hand straight back to your guard.\n• Wrap your hands and use gloves of the right weight for bag work.

1. Warm up for 10 minutes: joint circles, jumping jacks and gentle leg swings.
2. Keep a stable stance with your knees bent, your guard up and your weight on both feet.
3. Kick by lifting your knee first, then extend the leg and bring it back the same way before you put it down.
4. In Fortia, log the time of the session, for example 1:30:00, and the calories if your watch shows them.
• Stretch your hips and hamstrings after training, while you are warm, not cold before high kicks.\n• Control your techniques with partners: speed comes after precision.

1. Warm up for 10 minutes: arm and shoulder circles, then a few easy routes or traverses.
2. Climb with straight arms when you can, so your legs push you up and your arms just hold on.
3. Place your feet carefully on the holds with the tip of the shoe, and keep your hips close to the wall.
4. In Fortia, log the time you climbed, for example 1:30:00.

• Rest between hard routes: your forearms and fingers need a few minutes to recover.\n• Check knots, harness and belay device with your partner before every route; when bouldering, fall onto the mats.

1. Warm up with a few minutes of trunk rotations and arm swings, then some half swings with a short iron.
2. Set up with your feet shoulder-width apart, knees soft, bending forward from the hips with your back straight.
3. Turn your shoulders on the backswing, start the downswing with your hips and swing through to a balanced finish.
4. In Fortia, log the time of your round or practice, for example 4:00:00.
• Grip the club lightly: tension in your hands and arms costs speed and control.\n• Walking the course is part of the workout: pull a trolley instead of carrying a heavy bag on one shoulder.
